The record:
Write the overview of the executive synopsis for the incident on io-shop below: a short paragraph in plain words, for the people who lead the company rather than the engineers who responded - what happened, how long it lasted, what it cost the business and the people who responded, and how it was resolved.

What a reader saw: The slowest shop page loads slowed sharply for some shoppers
Why, in plain words: Switching on a new shop feature sent shoppers' pages through a calculation of their typical spend that likely does far more work the more purchases a shopper has made, so pages for shoppers with long purchase histories became very slow.

Figures:
- How long it lasted: 6m 19s {duration}
- What it cost the shop in takings (estimated by Argus): none {customer_loss}
- Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.

What was done to end it:
- Argus: reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature - confirmed, still in place
- Argus: proposed a fix, PR #573 - opened as a draft

Name {duration} and {customer_loss} in your overview.
Write no figure yourself - not in digits, not spelled out, and not as a word that sizes it ("a brief outage", "a minor loss", "tripled"). Where a figure goes, write its name, braces and all, and the synopsis writes the figure in.
Say nothing about how the incident was resolved beyond what the list of what was done says: a draft fix has not run, and nothing it would do has happened.
Speak of Argus by name, never as "we", "our" or "us": Argus is the system that responded, and each line of what was done says who did it.
Where you say who was affected, say which ones, as the cause does, or that some were, where it does not say which - never how many, and never all of them, where the cause does not say all.
Keep "likely" on what the cause says is likely, and only there.

Call submit_executive_overview with your overview.

The postmortem it is written from:
The slowest shop page loads slowed sharply for some shoppers while typical-purchase-feature was on
Incident: HighLatency on io-shop
Date: Nov 12, 2026, 14:16 to 14:22:19 UTC
Status: Draft. 1 of 6 action items are done.
Written by: Argus Postmortem agent, Nov 12, 2026, 14:27:45 UTC. Not reviewed yet. Each part is as of when the work it reports ended, which the timeline dates; who ended the incident is as of now.
First told: Argus posted in Slack, Nov 12, 2026, 14:22:02 UTC
Ended by: Argus: reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature - confirmed, still in place

Summary
The service broke at 14:16 UTC and was back to normal at 14:22:19 UTC, 6 minutes 19 seconds later. What its alert watches went from 199 ms before it began to 2081 ms at its worst. The shop's takings fell short of the same hours on earlier weeks by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all. Switching on a new shop feature sent shoppers' pages through a calculation of their typical spend that likely does far more work the more purchases a shopper has made, so pages for shoppers with long purchase histories became very slow. What Argus did: reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place. Argus opened a draft fix, PR #573, for a person to review and merge. If typical-purchase-feature is switched back on before a fix is in place, the slowest shop requests could slow down again in the same way.

Impact
6m 19s - onset until back to normal
1.0% to 1.6% - error rate, before onset and while broken on average (no rise)
199 ms to 1396 ms - what the alert watches, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 2081 ms; the rule's line is 500 ms)
none - customer loss (estimated)

Root cause and contributing factors
With typical-purchase-feature on, render_spend_summary calls typical_spend_per_item (src/io_shop/typical_spend.py). That function finds the middle price by removing the smallest remaining price over and over until it reaches the middle, and each min and each remove is a full pass over the list. Its work therefore grows far faster than the length of a shopper's purchase history, so requests for shoppers with long histories became very slow while requests for most shoppers stayed fast. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
Causal chain
symptom Shoppers' slowest requests took much longer to load. The alert fired on the slowest tail of request durations across the service's replicas, and the Investigator placed the start at the onset. Failed requests did not rise: the account page error rate stayed within its usual range and peaked before the onset.
  Evidence:
    AL1 p99 latency above threshold for 5m
    T5 14:22:05 Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 14:16
    Gbac1 WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 35 occurrences in 36 minutes, 13:46–14:21; # was 0.50% to 2.50%, typically 1.00%, highest at 14:02
why 1 Requests began running the code path behind typical-purchase-feature. Admin switched the flag on at 14:15:47 UTC. Before that, every flag evaluation logged came back off. In the minute of the switch the evaluations were mixed, and from the onset on, every evaluation logged came back on.
  Evidence:
    P1 14:15:47 UTC flag toggle typical-purchase-feature by admin: feature flag typical-purchase-feature was switched on
    Ga6f5 INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=off - 200 evaluations - 29 occurrences in 29 minutes, 13:46–14:14
    Gc8c4 INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=off 163 / on 37 - 200 evaluations - 1 occurrence in 1 minute, 14:15
    Gd44a INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=on - 200 evaluations - 7 occurrences in 7 minutes, 14:16–14:22
  Ruled out:
    A deploy or release on the service: the Investigator Agent asked for production change events - deploys and releases, and flag changes from the flag provider's history, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 12 14:17; the Investigator Agent read back 1 production change.
      T7
      T8
    Any other flag change: the flag provider's history for the hour before showed no flag change by anyone but Argus other than this one.
      T14 14:22:18 Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 1 flag change by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 14:22:17
why 2 With the flag on, the account page's spend summary calls a typical-spend calculation whose work, by Code-Fix's reading, grows far faster than the length of a shopper's purchase history, so shoppers with long histories waited much longer.
  Evidence:
    U1 typical_spend_per_item at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:67, in render_spend_summary: calls it: return typical_spend_per_item(account)
    F1 What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
Contributing factors
- The flag went straight from off for every evaluation to on for every evaluation. No staged rollout to a small share of shoppers was seen, and no automatic guard that turns a just-changed flag off when latency rises was seen. (AI-3, AI-4)
- No test or check of how the flagged code path performs with long purchase histories was seen before the flag was switched on in production. (AI-5)

Hypotheses considered
 | Hypothesis | Confidence | Result
C1 | Feature flag typical-purchase-feature was switched on at 14:15:47 UTC. p99 latency jumped from about 200ms to 1000-2000ms from 14:16 UTC, while p50, p95, error rate, memory and CPU stayed at baseline. No deploy occurred, the rollout and pods were unchanged, and the dependencies show no failure. | 0.88 | confirmed

Trigger
typical-purchase-feature flag went from OFF to ON at 14:15:47 UTC, by admin.

Resolution
 | Time (UTC) | Action | By | Kind | Outcome
M1 | 14:22:19 | Reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature for C1 | Argus | can be put back | confirmed, still in place
 | 14:26:07 | Proposed a fix: PR #573 | Code-Fix Agent | nothing to put back | opened as a draft

Detection
The incident on io-shop began at 14:16 UTC. HighLatency fired at 14:22 UTC, 6 minutes later.
What the alert said
AL1 | p99 latency above threshold for 5m

Action items
Item | Action | Type | Owner | Tracking | Status
AI-1 | Reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature | mitigate | Argus | - | done
AI-2 | Review and merge the proposed fix | prevent | unassigned | PR #573 | open
AI-3 | Roll out io-shop feature flag changes to a small share of traffic first, rather than to every request at once. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-4 | Add an automatic guard that switches a recently changed io-shop flag back off when tail request latency rises after the change. | mitigate | unassigned | - | open
AI-5 | Require a cost-bounding test with large inputs, such as long purchase histories, for code behind a feature flag before that flag can be switched on in production. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-6 | Route the io-shop HighLatency alert to the on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires. | process | unassigned | - | open

Lessons learned
What went well
- The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
- 17 seconds after the alert was raised, the Investigator Agent formed 1 candidate cause, best first: C1.
- 19 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature for C1, moved from ON to OFF.
- 3 minutes 8 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent judged the action CONFIRMED.
- 4 minutes 7 seconds after the alert was raised, the Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #573.
What went wrong
- Nobody was paged: the alert was not linked to any on-call incident, so no person was brought in while the incident ran.
Where it got lucky
Nothing.

Timeline (UTC)
 | Nov 12 14:16 | IMPACT BEGINS | the incident began

T1 | 14:22:02 |  | Argus Received HighLatency on io-shop

T16 | 14:22:19 | MITIGATION APPLIED | Mitigation Agent Reverted the feature flag typical-purchase-feature for C1, moved from ON to OFF

Response effort
none - engineer time
192,420 - tokens spent by Argus

Supporting information
The incident's walk: http://localhost:8000/incidents/7530557b-4e8d-4c98-94b0-9cdfd0bf1744
The fix it proposed: PR #573 (https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/573) opened as a draft. The record holds nothing about it after that.
Changes to production read
P1 | 14:15:47 UTC flag toggle typical-purchase-feature by admin: feature flag typical-purchase-feature was switched on
Deploys read, none came back.
Log messages read (UTC)
Ga6f5 | INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=off - 200 evaluations - 29 occurrences in 29 minutes, 13:46–14:14
G46bc | ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 56 occurrences in 36 minutes, 13:46–14:21
Gbac1 | WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 35 occurrences in 36 minutes, 13:46–14:21; # was 0.50% to 2.50%, typically 1.00%, highest at 14:02
Gad41 | INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 2 occurrences in 26 minutes, 13:57–14:22
Gc8c4 | INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=off 163 / on 37 - 200 evaluations - 1 occurrence in 1 minute, 14:15
Gd44a | INFO io-shop: typical-purchase-feature=on - 200 evaluations - 7 occurrences in 7 minutes, 14:16–14:22
What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
F1 | The fault: typical_spend_per_item in src/io_shop/typical_spend.py found the middle price by calling remaining.remove(min(remaining)) (n-1)//2 times. Each min and each remove is a full pass over the list, so a history of n purchases costs about n² comparisons. Most histories are short, so the cost lands only on shoppers with long ones. That matches the investigation: p99 jumped while p50 and p95 stayed at baseline once typical-purchase-feature sent requests down this path (render_spend_summary in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py calls it when use_typical_spend is set). The flag only exposed the fault; the function itself is the fault.

The fix sorts the prices once and returns the element at index (n-1)//2. That is the same lower-of-two-middles element the old loop returned (repeated prices still count once per purchase), and it costs O(n log n). An empty history still raises ValueError, as min([]) did before, so callers see no change in what is raised. The signature and return value are unchanged, so render_spend_summary and the account page need no change.

The test: tests/io_shop/test_typical_spend.py keeps every existing correctness case. It adds a case that counts comparisons on a 2,001-purchase history, using an int subclass whose __lt__ increments a counter, and asserts the count stays under 30 per purchase. The old repeated-min loop does roughly 1.5 million comparisons on that input, far over the bound. A single sort does a few tens of thousands, within it. The test also checks that the returned middle is still correct. Counting comparisons rather than timing keeps the test independent of how fast the machine is.
How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main
U1 | typical_spend_per_item at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:67, in render_spend_summary: calls it: return typical_spend_per_item(account)
Assumptions
- Exchange rate: EUR converted at 0.92191 per USD, published 2026-11-11
- No engineer minutes: no on-call incident was linked to this one, so nobody was paged to respond

Review checklist
✓ Key incident data collected (met)
✓ Impact assessed (met)
○ Root-cause analysis complete (for a person)
  running the proposed fix's tests against the current code would confirm the reading, not that the code it reads is what ran (AI-2)
○ Every action item owned and dated (for a person)
○ Reviewed and shared (for a person)

The document, by field:
overview: For {duration}, the slowest shop pages on io-shop became much slower for some shoppers. A new shop feature had been switched on, and it sent shoppers' pages through a calculation of their typical spend. That calculation likely does far more work the more purchases a shopper has made, so pages became very slow for shoppers with long purchase histories. Argus estimates the shop lost {customer_loss} in takings. Responders were not disturbed: no on-call incident was linked to this one, so nobody was paged. Argus ended the problem by switching the new feature back off, and it confirmed that the feature remains off. Argus has also proposed a lasting fix, but it is only an unapproved draft and has not been put into use.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {duration}, are figures code writes in from the list of figures in the ask. They are not judged.
  - The overview is written in plain words for the people who lead the company. A claim said more plainly than the postmortem says it is grounded where it means the same.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
